messages.subject_clean: Difference in hg19 and GRCh37 reference genomes
messages.body_plain:
I would like to preface this by saying that I've grown to love featureCounts, and think its documentation and reporting is the best.
 I was wondering if a marked difference has been observed when using featureCounts with the hg19 and ensembl GRCh37 reference genomes. I aligned my reads using STAR and got similar results using each reference genome. I then go to use featureCounts and get vastly difference results. Using the hg19 genome in featureCounts I get about 40-50% successfully assigned fragments, whereas when using the GRCh37 genome I get about 70-80% successfully assigned fragments. I'm concerned that the significant difference means I'm implementing something wrong in featureCounts, and am confused as to which output I should trust. Any advice or guidance would be greatly appreciated. Thank you!

messages.body_plain:
Hi Gregory,

I suspect there is a mismatch between the chromosome names in the reference genome compared to those in the annotation file used by featureCounts.

While hg19 and GRCh37 are the same genome build, UCSC appends "chr" to the beginning of the chromosome names, e.g. chr1, chr2, etc. On the other hand, Ensembl leaves the chromosomes as is: 1, 2, etc.  Another difference is the mitochondrial genome, which UCSC labels chrM and Ensembl labels MT.

What are the chromosome names in the annotation file you are using with feature counts?

John

messages.subject: Re: Very slow processing last step using -I 100
messages.subject_clean: Very slow processing last step using -I 100
messages.body_plain:
Hi Dylan,

The "-I 100" option turned on the read re-assembly step in the Subread aligner for detecting long insertions and deletions (16bp or longer), and this step is relatively slower. A 3-5 hour running time is pretty normal when processing a high-coverage data set (like ~15 millions of reads from an RNA-seq sample). Also, we haven't make this step multi-threaded, hence it only runs on one CPU. You can avoid the read re-assembly step by specifying an "-I" option less than 16, or ignore this option.

The FASTA file contains the read assemblies where one or more indels were detected. General read assemblies from Subread are several hundred bases long, hence you have thousands of them. If you look at the name fields in the FASTA file, you can find the start location and the end location of this assembly on the chromosome, and also a CIGAR-formatted string for indicating the locations of indels detected in this assembly.

Cheers,
Yang

Hi,

We ran into a weird issue when trying to filter to primary alignments when running featureCounts (from `subread-1.5.0-p3`). We aligned samples with HISAT2 to hg38 and quantified Gencode v25.

Here is the output with NO primary filter
> featureCounts  -s 2 -p -T 8 -a gencode.v25.annotationGRCh38.gtf  -o ${ID}_Gencode.v25.hg38_Genes.counts $BAM

Assigned 13185409
Unassigned_Ambiguity 965509
Unassigned_MultiMapping 11102556
Unassigned_NoFeatures 15641266
Unassigned_Secondary 0

Here is the output with the primary filter
> featureCounts  -s 2 -p -T 8 -a gencode.v25.annotationGRCh38.gtf --primary -o ${ID}_Gencode.v25.hg38_Genes.counts $BAM

Assigned 13944085
Unassigned_Ambiguity 1307782
Unassigned_MultiMapping 0
Unassigned_NoFeatures 17524718
Unassigned_Secondary 8118155

However, the manual describes primary alignments as those with the 0x100 flag in the BAM file. We get very different assignment rates when creating our own BAM file of primary alignments

> samtools view -@ 8 -bh -F 0x100 $BAM > $TMPBAM
> samtools index $TMPBAM
> featureCounts  -s 2 -p -T 8 -a gencode.v25.annotationGRCh38.gtf  -o ${ID}_Gencode.v25.hg38_Genes.counts $TMPBAM

Assigned 13182941
Unassigned_Ambiguity 964886
Unassigned_MultiMapping 3289714
Unassigned_NoFeatures 15634373
Unassigned_Secondary 0

Why would we not get the same fragments assigned when filtering the BAM file above? Is there some step that first sorts the BAM file by alignment score and then takes the highest scoring alignment as the primary?

Thanks,
Andrew

messages.subject: Re: Discrepancies with "primary" alignments
messages.subject_clean: Discrepancies with "primary" alignments
messages.body_plain:
Hi Andrew,

Firstly, could you please update your copy of Subread package to its latest version 1.5.2? There are a lot of changes made since the release of 1.5.0-p3.

By default, featureCounts does not count multi-mapping reads. However when you choose to count primary alignments only, featureCounts will count multi-mapping reads as long as they are marked as primary alignments. Those multi-mapping reads marked as secondary alignments will not be counted and they were put into the category 'Unassigned_Secondary'. Therefore in your second run you see alignments assigned this category but no alignments assigned to category 'Unassigned_MultiMapping'.

In your third run, you did not specify that you will count primary alignments only in your command. Therefore featureCounts did not count multi-mapping reads and you can see there are alignments assigned to 'Unassigned_MultiMapping' category. The 'Unassigned_Secondary' category contains no reads since your bam file only includes primary alignments.

Best regards,

Wei

messages.subject: Re: Discrepancies with "primary" alignments
messages.subject_clean: Discrepancies with "primary" alignments
messages.body_plain:
featureCounts only uses the 0x100 flag to look for primary alignments.

The main difference between your 2nd and 3rd runs is that multi-mapping reads were counted in your 2nd run but they were not counted in your 3rd run. featureCounts uses 'NH' tag to look for multi-mapping reads.

If you add '-M' option to your command in the 3rd run you will get much closer results. This option allows multi-mapping reads to be counted.

Best regards,

Wei
